opus-5.5.text:
I think the basic case comes down to the sheer size of the prize. If you look at the world economy, something like half or more of global GDP is paid out as compensation to workers. That's on the order of fifty to sixty trillion dollars a year. So if you could build systems that can do a large fraction of that work, even partially substituting for human labor across cognitive and eventually physical tasks, the value you capture is enormous. Against that backdrop, spending a few trillion dollars a year on compute, data centers, chip fabs, and energy infrastructure doesn't look crazy. It looks like a reasonable investment relative to the returns.

And it's not just about capturing the existing wage bill. The more interesting part is what happens to growth. Historically, one of the main constraints on economic growth has been that labor is a fixed input. You can't easily scale up the number of researchers, engineers, or workers. Population grows slowly. But if AI systems can substitute for labor, then labor effectively becomes something you can accumulate the way you accumulate capital. You build more compute, you get more workers. That breaks a key bottleneck, and standard growth models suggest you could get dramatically faster growth rates, potentially an order of magnitude above what we see today.

So when people hear "trillions of dollars a year" they think it sounds wildly excessive, but I'd frame it the other way around. If you take seriously the possibility that these systems become broadly capable, the current levels of investment are, if anything, quite modest relative to the economic value at stake. The question isn't really whether it's worth it in the abstract. It's how confident you are that the technology will get there, and how quickly. And I think there's a reasonably good case that we're on a trajectory where that kind of spending is justified.

r001.rationale: The response highlights the enormous wage bill as an investment opportunity, but does not identify labor as the most expensive factor of production.

r002.rationale: It says AI substitution could remove labor as a growth bottleneck and produce dramatically faster growth rates.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the way I'd frame it is that labor is by far the largest input into the global economy. If you look at total output, something like 60 percent of it goes to compensating workers. Globally, that's on the order of 50 or 60 trillion dollars a year flowing to people in exchange for their labor. So if you develop a technology that can perform a large share of the tasks that humans currently get paid to do, the value you're competing for is enormous. In that light, spending a few trillion dollars a year on compute, data centers, chips, and energy isn't extravagant at all. It's actually a fairly modest fraction of the prize.

The second point is that AI differs from past technologies in a specific way. Historically, when we automated something, we automated a narrow task. We replaced the loom operator or the switchboard operator, and then the economy shifted labor into other things. What's distinctive about current AI systems is that they're general. They can be applied to a very wide range of cognitive work, and increasingly, through robotics, to physical work as well. If you believe that these systems will eventually be substitutable for human workers across most tasks, then the returns on capital don't diminish the way they normally do. Normally, when you build more factories, you run out of workers to staff them, and that caps your returns. But if you can produce the workers themselves by building more compute, you remove that bottleneck. Capital accumulation can then drive growth in a way it never could before.

And then there's the question of what that means for growth rates. The standard economic models, when you plug in a technology that lets you substitute capital for labor across the board, predict not just a one-time boost but a sustained acceleration. Growth rates could be several times what we've seen in the last century. If that's even partially right, the return on infrastructure investment is extraordinary. You're not building something that earns a normal rate of return. You're building something that could reshape the entire trajectory of the economy.

I'd also stress that the infrastructure is genuinely the binding constraint right now. The algorithms and the software scale pretty well. What limits how much AI work gets done is how many chips you have, how much electricity you can deliver to them, and how fast you can build the facilities to house them. Those are slow, capital-intensive things. If you want the benefits to arrive this decade rather than in several decades, you have to make those investments early, and at scale.

Now, I don't want to pretend there's no uncertainty. The capabilities might plateau. Deployment might be slower than the technology permits, because of regulation or institutional inertia or just how long it takes firms to reorganize around new tools. In that case, some of these investments would look like a bubble. But I think the expected value calculation still favors investment, because the downside is that you've overbuilt some data centers, and the upside is that you've accelerated the arrival of a technology that could make the world dramatically richer. Those aren't symmetric outcomes.

r001.rationale: It says labor is the economy’s largest input, with 60% of output going to worker compensation, and uses the value of automating that labor to justify spending trillions on AI infrastructure.

r002.rationale: It says economic models predict sustained acceleration when capital can substitute for labor, with growth rates potentially several times those of the last century.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the key is to compare that spending with the economic value of the labor you could automate. Labor accounts for a very large share of economic output. So if AI can perform even a modest fraction of that work reliably, the value could be enormous. Spending trillions of dollars a year on infrastructure could make sense if it enables services worth substantially more than that.

And the opportunity isn’t just to do the same work more cheaply. If you make skilled labor much more abundant, you can do things that currently aren’t affordable: provide more tutoring, carry out more research, develop more software. One particularly important possibility is accelerating scientific and technological progress, which could raise productivity across the rest of the economy.

Of course, that’s a conditional argument. You need systems that actually perform useful tasks, and the costs of deploying them have to be low enough. There are also separate questions about safety and who benefits. But the basic economic case is that labor is such a large part of the economy that even very expensive infrastructure could be a worthwhile investment.

r001.rationale: The response says labor accounts for a large share of economic output, but does not identify labor as the most expensive factor of production.

r002.rationale: The response says scientific and technological progress could raise productivity, but does not clearly state that automating labor is likely to accelerate economic growth.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic reason is that labor is an enormous part of the world economy. We spend tens of trillions of dollars a year on people doing cognitive work, so even a modest improvement in how productively that work gets done could be worth trillions of dollars annually.

And the potential goes beyond doing existing tasks more cheaply. If you can make high-quality cognitive labor much more abundant, you could do more scientific research, develop medicines faster, and provide education and other services to many more people. Those are potentially very large benefits.

Of course, that doesn’t mean any particular trillion-dollar investment is justified. You need systems that are reliable enough to do economically valuable work, and the value they produce has to exceed the cost of building and operating the infrastructure. There are also serious questions about safety, displacement, and who receives the gains. But the scale of the opportunity makes investment at that level economically plausible.

r001.rationale: The response says labor accounts for tens of trillions of dollars in cognitive work, but does not identify labor as the most expensive factor of production.

r002.rationale: The response describes potential productivity gains and broader benefits, but does not clearly state that automating labor is likely to accelerate economic growth.
